new_statements.second_reader_evidence: VERBATIM CHECK of the reader's quotes (viewed as page images of scan pages 11-12 and): all three are there. p.55 §4.2 Vowels: "Vowels tend to be longer in stressed final position than elsewhere in words of the same number of syllables." p.56 /ɛ/ allophone (ə): "Voiced mid close central un-rounded vocoid occurs in unstressed second syllable in multi-syllable words following non-dental laterals following /ɛ/ in initial syllable." (line-break hyphen in "un-rounded" only). Orthography chart last row: "/ˊ/ (stress)... is unmarked.. is unmarked". The examples with final acute (pimí, wɛmbí, kuní, ɛpí, ouní, olsín...) and non-final ɛndéim are as reported. NEW: THE FULL PAPER IS NOW IN HAND. web.arc…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated in the accessible pages: the authors list stress (acute /ˊ/) among the phonemes, i.e. treat it as contrastive and mark it on every phonemic form, and refer to 'stressed final position' and to 'unstressed second syllable' in multi-syllable words. In the marked examples and the sample text the stress mark falls on the final syllable in the large majority of words (pimí, wɛmbí, kuní, ɛpí, ouní, olsín, rokú, nonomún, kongonúm, tonú, turúm, konú, tumbá, ením, maní, multún) but not always (ɛndéim 'one'; mbálus and mbalús 'airplane' both on p.77). The dedicated stress section (somewhere in pp. 60-76, not scanned) would settle whether stress is predictable (final) or lexical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in the accessible pages; only one acute per word is marked in the examples seen.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in the accessible pages; the sample text (p.77) shows the same word 'airplane' as mbálus and mbalús.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: phonemic transcriptions of citation forms (pp. 46-59) and a connected sample text (pp. 77-78); the orthography leaves stress unmarked.
new_statements.identity_note: The only description is of the Nii (Ek Nii) language of the Western Highlands as worked on by the SIL Stucky team (Glottolog niii1240, ISO nii); the accessible pages name no dialect or village. Glottolog reference 36533 mislabels the volume as 'Studies in languages of the Ok family'; the SIL catalog line printed on the scans gives the actual volume title 'Phonologies of three languages of Papua New Guinea' (WPNGL 2, 108 pp.).

sources.note: Stress is treated as a phoneme (orthography chart last row: '/ˊ/ (stress)... is unmarked'); p.55: 'Vowels tend to be longer in stressed final position than elsewhere in words of the same number of syllables'; pp.56 and 59 describe vowel allophones 'in unstressed second syllable in multi-syllable words'; every phonemic example and the pp.77-78 sample text carry acute stress marks, overwhelmingly on the final syllable (pimí 'bee', wɛmbí 'snake', kuní 'food', olsín 'yesterday', rokú 'tobacco', nonomún 'they will eat', tonú, turúm, konú, tumbá, ením, multún) with a few non-final marks (ɛndéim 'on…
Phoneme inventory only (notes the three laterals); nothing on stress or tone; cites Stucky & Stucky 1973 with the SIL PDF URL above and Foley 1986 p.63.
